title: The Science and Politics of a Warming World: Inside the Struggle for Global Climate Consensus
content: Earth’s climate, defined by long-term weather averages (30+ years), falls into five major types and is driven by interactions among five planetary systems: solar energy, Earth's shape and tilt, wind and ocean currents, and the greenhouse effect. While natural processes have shaped the planet's climate over millions of years, human activities, specifically the release of heat-trapping atmospheric greenhouse gases, have been the primary driver of rapid global warming since the Industrial Revolution. Addressing global climate change relies on a broad network of international institutions spanning United Nations bodies, scientific panels, financial mechanisms, and local networks, led by key UN agencies such as the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) (Bonn, Germany), and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) (Geneva, Switzerland). Specifically, UN climate summits, officially known as the Conference of the Parties (COP), serve as the supreme decision-making body of the UNFCCC (Bonn, Germany). Although three decades of these summits (from COP1 in 1995 to COP31 in November 2026) have established a robust global diplomatic framework, they have consistently struggled to enforce decisive actions, such as deep emissions cuts and the phasing out of fossil fuels. Most notably, following a record-long session, the COP31 UN climate summit failed on November 22, 2026, unable to secure an agreement on the Antalya Pact due to sharp divisions over fossil fuels and climate funding. This paper is structured to: (i) introduce the fundamentals of Earth's climate; (ii) examine the primary drivers of climate change; (iii) highlight key institutions involved in global climate governance; (iv) provide insights into the UNFCCC (Bonn, Germany) by reviewing the core goals, major achievements, and key shortcomings of its COP summits; (v) examine the failures of the COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, and critically analyze their underlying causes; and (vi) summarize key takeaways and outline a strategic path forward. In summary, the failure of the COP31 summit stems from several interconnected factors: disputes over omitting fossil fuel phase-outs, a deadlock on climate finance, deep divides among major economies, resistance from major fossil fuel producers and developing giants, the leadership vacuum left by the absence of the United States, shifting geopolitics combined with strict consensus rules, and disagreements regarding carbon capture, draft texts, and IPCC (Geneva, Switzerland) findings.
